clue.text: In stupid form, a chore to translate?

definitions.text: In stupid form, a chore to translate?

indicators.note: letters put into a stupid, muddled form are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolchild groans that translating this Latin text is a stupid chore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In stupid form' rearranges A CHORE. The whole clue is also the definition: the Roman poet is the classic set text that schoolchildren found a chore to translate.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman lyric poet's Odes were a standard Latin translation exercise at school, so pupils often found the work a chore.

clue.text: Who dares to deviate round motorway? That's not Bill Bailey's route

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go round the motorway letter, enclosing it
to deviate is to stray from the set course, so these letters stray into a new order

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Someone daring takes a detour around the motorway, which is not the way Bill Bailey goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to deviate' rearranges WHO DARES, and 'round' puts that around M. The old song pleads 'Won't you come home, Bill Bailey?', so Bill Bailey famously did not head back.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song Bill Bailey stays away and will not come home, so a route towards one's house is exactly what he avoided.

clue.text: Puzzles they select on the basis of size

definitions.meaning: enigmas or conundrums posed as questions

definitions.text: they select on the basis of size
definitions.meaning: coarse sieves sort soil or gravel, letting small pieces through and holding back large ones

explanation.definitionFit: Conundrums are posed puzzles, and coarse sieves for gravel separate material by size.

clue.text: City appears smart to Lady Stanhope

parts.note: chic means smart or stylish
Lady Hester Stanhope was the famous English traveller and adventurer in the Middle East

explanation.surface: A city strikes a famous Georgian lady traveller as fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Hester Stanhope (1776-1839) was an English aristocrat who travelled and lived in the Levant.
explanation.definitionFit: This cathedral city in West Sussex is the county town there, a city in the plain sense.

clue.text: Water flow barrier impedes a good deal, maybe

indicators.note: the barrier word stands in the way, getting inside the other pieces to block them

parts.note: a sale is an example of a good deal for shoppers
a dam is a barrier holding back the flow of a river

explanation.surface: A dam built across the river gets in the way of a profitable deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impedes' works because a dam blocks a flow by standing in its way. ADAM'S ALE is an old joke name: Adam in Eden had only water to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular old name for plain drinking water, the only drink the first man in Eden had.

clue.text: Commonly busy, but first face rigorous enquiry into truth

indicators.note: first tells us the face word comes at the front, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: a dial is the face of a clock or watch

indicators.note: commonly means in a common accent that drops initial aitches, so the busy word loses its opening letter

parts.note: hectic means busy and frantic

explanation.surface: Someone who is always busy is urged to first face up to some tough questioning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' imitates a Cockney accent that drops the H, giving ECTIC; 'first' sets the clock face ahead. 'face' looks like a verb (to confront) but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialectic is the philosophical method of seeking truth through reasoned argument and counter-argument.

clue.text: Bookmaker found where the race starts

definitions.meaning: a maker of a book, here the evangelist who wrote the second Gospel
runners line up on the starting line

explanation.definitionFit: The evangelist wrote a Gospel, a book of the Bible, and the starting line in athletics bears this name too.

clue.text: Discharge whole group of busy workers — it's in all the papers

parts.note: an arc is an electrical discharge leaping across a gap
a hive holds the whole colony of busy worker bees

explanation.surface: A firm sacks its entire workforce and the story is in every newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy workers' are bees, a crossword favourite. The held text has 'alf' where the page prints 'all'.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of historical records and documents kept together is a store of old papers.

clue.text: Written work in mess may lose marks

indicators.note: to lose things is to be without them, so the marks are taken out of the words

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for mark, the old German currency, so two marks give two Ms

explanation.surface: A piece of written work done in a messy way might lose marks from the teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lose' takes the two Ms out of MESS MAY, leaving ESS and AY. The surface makes 'marks' look like school grades.
explanation.definitionFit: A short prose composition on a subject is a standard piece of written schoolwork.

clue.text: Fast runner often in form

definitions.meaning: a swift animal, the long-eared runner of the fields
a form is the shallow hollow in grass where this animal lies

explanation.definitionFit: The animal is famously fast, and it rests in a grass hollow called a form.

clue.text: Admire a newly cooked cake

indicators.note: cooking something up anew means rearranging its letters into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone praises a cake fresh from the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'newly cooked' rearranges ADMIRE A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain sponge traditionally eaten with a glass of fortified wine from the Portuguese island, hence its name.

clue.text: Extinct bovine creature, or its modern counterpart, roughly speaking

indicators.note: roughly speaking means the words, said aloud, only approximately sound like the answer

parts.note: or gives OR; an ox is the domestic cattle of today, descended from the extinct wild beast

explanation.surface: A clue writer contrasts an extinct wild beast with its living descendant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly speaking' says OR OX aloud: the ox is the modern counterpart of the extinct beast.
explanation.definitionFit: The great wild ox of Europe, ancestor of domestic cattle, died out in Poland in 1627.

clue.text: Appreciative cry to hooker? That's rich

definitions.meaning: praise shouted at the rugby player in the scrum who heels the ball back, 'Nicely heeled!'

explanation.walkthrough: In rugby union the hooker, in the front row of the scrum, strikes the ball back with the heel. 'Hooker' tempts a quite different reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means wealthy, from the idea of wearing good shoes with sound heels.

clue.text: Minute is short time as part of year

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
in means as part of, included within

explanation.surface: A minute is only a brief moment within a whole year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' looks like a unit of time to match 'time' and 'year', but it is the adjective meaning very small.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute pronounced my-NEWT means extremely small, a synonym of little.

clue.text: Bob may seem less attractive with this quibble

definitions.text: Bob may seem less attractive with this
definitions.meaning: a bob haircut looks scruffy when the ends of the hair are frayed and divided

explanation.definitionFit: To argue over trivial distinctions is the idiom; split ends of hair would spoil a neat bob.

clue.text: Tries to stop son entering repeated exams

indicators.note: the son letter enters the exams word, going inside it

parts.note: resits are exams taken again after failing

explanation.surface: A parent tries to stop their son going in for yet more exam retakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' puts S inside RESITS.
explanation.definitionFit: To withstand or oppose something is to try to stop it.

clue.text: Gloomy sort of wave at vessel coming in

indicators.note: the vessel pieces come inside the wave word

parts.note: a sine wave is the smooth repeating wave of mathematics and physics
an urn is a vessel, such as a large vase

explanation.surface: A sullen person gives a half-hearted wave as a ship arrives in port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming in' signals the insertion. 'vessel' suggests a ship arriving in port, but it is a vase-like container; 'sort of wave' is the mathematician's curve, not a hand gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturnine means sullen and morose, from the planet's supposed melancholy influence.

clue.text: Headgear VIP doesn't have on

indicators.note: doesn't have means a part is missing, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a very important person is a top person

explanation.surface: An important dignitary turns up without wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't have' removes ON from TOP PERSON, leaving the plural for top hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Toppers are tall silk top hats, a kind of formal hat.

clue.text: Be defensive — play for time after losing one wicket

definitions.meaning: to block or refuse to cooperate, giving nothing away

definitions.text: play for time after losing one wicket
definitions.meaning: a cricket batsman who has seen a wicket fall bats very cautiously to avoid getting out

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batting side that loses a wicket may bat slowly and safely to survive, rather than scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to obstruct or delay by evasive tactics, and in cricket to bat purely defensively.

clue.text: How one may use Internet, say? That's excessive

definitions.note: the clue gives the adjective, while the answer is the noun for an excessive amount

indicators.note: say means the phrase is spoken aloud, giving a sound like the answer

parts.note: one browses the web, or surfs it

explanation.surface: Someone browsing online asks how to use the web, and is told it is too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the homophone: 'surf it', what one does to the web, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfeit is an excess or overabundance, more than is needed.

clue.text: Bun with clean seafood

parts.note: a bread roll is a bun
to mop is to clean, as a floor

explanation.surface: A bun is served alongside some fresh seafood.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollmop is a pickled herring fillet rolled round onion, a kind of fish dish.

clue.text: Windy place, cold for Romans here in the past

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
hic is the Latin word for here
ago means in the past, as in long ago

explanation.surface: A breezy spot was too chilly for the Romans who lived there long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For Romans' signals Latin. The US city is nicknamed the Windy City.
explanation.definitionFit: The US city on Lake Michigan is nicknamed the Windy City, so it is a breezy place.

clue.text: Commissioned doctors turning up in a very minor case — most impressive

indicators.note: the doctors go in the small case, inside its letters

parts.note: wee means very small, minor

indicators.note: turning up in a down clue means reading the word backwards, from the bottom

parts.note: MOs are medical officers, commissioned officers in the armed forces

explanation.surface: Army doctors respond to a tiny medical case, which proves deeply impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses, giving SOM, since a down answer reads upward; 'in' and 'case' make A WEE the box holding it. MOs are military doctors, which is why they are 'commissioned'.
explanation.definitionFit: Awesome means inspiring awe, so extremely impressive.

clue.text: As economist, make distinctive mark on hard currency

definitions.meaning: John Stuart ... was the Victorian economist and philosopher

definitions.text: make distinctive mark on hard currency
definitions.meaning: to put ridges round the edge of a coin

explanation.walkthrough: Hard currency here means coins, whose ridged edges are milled.
explanation.definitionFit: The economist John Stuart Mill, and the verb for ridging coin edges.

clue.text: Thought doctor should be put out of practice

indicators.note: the doctor is placed outside the practice word, surrounding it

parts.note: MD is Doctor of Medicine
use means practice or custom, as in usage

explanation.surface: Someone reflects that a doctor ought to be struck off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'should be put out of' places MD outside USE. The surface suggests a doctor struck off.
explanation.definitionFit: Mused means pondered or reflected.

clue.text: Sportsman having run in heat let it slip

indicators.note: the run letter goes in the shuffled letters
letting letters slip means they slide out of place into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: An athlete running in a qualifying heat lets the lead slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slip' rearranges HEAT LET IT, and 'in' puts R inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A triathlete is a sportsman who competes in swimming, cycling and running events.

clue.text: Take part of special sole to boot

indicators.note: the answer forms part of the words, running across them

explanation.surface: Take a section of a special shoe sole, as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' points to the letters running across 'special sole'. 'boot' suggests footwear, but 'to boot' means in addition.
explanation.definitionFit: To boot is an idiom for additionally or besides.

clue.text: Almost pot wild animal

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a crock is an earthenware pot

explanation.surface: Something nearly smashes a pot of a savage beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' removes the final K from CROCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Croc is short for crocodile, a large wild reptile.

clue.text: Take strong drink, since about to face excellent warrior

indicators.note: to face means coming before and looking towards the last piece
about means turned round, so the drink and the since words are read backwards together

parts.note: rum is a strong spirit
as means since, as in 'as you're here'
A1 means excellent, first-class, written AI

explanation.surface: Someone is told to drink a stiff spirit since they are about to meet a great fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the drink and 'since' round together, giving SAMUR; 'to face' sets it before A1 (written AI), the old Lloyd's Register mark for first-class. 'Take' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A samurai was a member of Japan's feudal military class, a warrior.

clue.text: Biased view given little weight by a philosopher

parts.note: spin is a slanted presentation of facts
oz is the abbreviation for ounce, a small weight

explanation.surface: A thinker's slanted opinion is given little weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Baruch Spinoza was a 17th-century Dutch rationalist philosopher.

clue.text: Showed how Romans would have liked to have seen Scotland?

definitions.text: how Romans would have liked to have seen Scotland?
definitions.meaning: rid of the Picts, the northern tribes who harried Roman Britain

explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were the tribes of northern Scotland whom the Romans never subdued; split as DE-PICTED, the answer means 'with the Picts removed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Portrayed or represented in a picture or words.

clue.text: 25 making a crescendo

parts.note: a swell is a gradual increase in loudness

explanation.surface: A passage of music builds to a crescendo.
explanation.walkthrough: '25' means the answer to 25 down, which this answer also means.
explanation.definitionFit: Clue 25's answer means in addition or too, a synonym of this phrase.
